subject: D60E2E5B3B2C4B2796B8B06FF4D08157
introduction: Ḥuqúqu’lláh, “the Right of God”, is the law of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas by which a believer pays nineteen per cent of what is left after a year’s necessary expenses, once it passes a set threshold. The guide’s sixty passages show two things held together throughout: the payment is an obligation revealed in the Book, and no one may demand it. Bahá’u’lláh for years declined to accept it, forbade its solicitation, and told His trustees to receive only what was given “with joy and radiance”. The rest is the working of the law: what is exempt, how it is reckoned, who may receive it. The tithe of Leviticus and Malachi, the Qur’an’s fifth and its alms that “purify”, are the earlier forms; Chronicles’ “of thine own have we given thee” and Paul’s “cheerful giver” state the spirit. Malachi’s “will a man rob God?”, the story of Ananias and Jesus’s tithers of mint are the cautions.
questions: The Ḥuqúq is obligatory and may not be demanded. What kind of obligation is that, and why would a religion choose it?
“Of thine own have we given thee.” What changes when giving is understood as returning?
The readings say payment purifies the remaining wealth and brings blessing. How do you understand that without making it a bargain?
Why do the readings take such care over receipts and trustees?
What did Jesus fault in those who tithed exactly?

outside.why: The Ḥuqúq depends on the willingness of the individual. Not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
If mutual help matters so among people, how much more what is God’s. All things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.
Action must occur with willingness. The people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the Lord.
If someone owned the whole world and gave it unwillingly, it would not be accepted. This poor widow hath cast in more than they all.
Demanding the Ḥuqúq is not permitted. Freely ye have received, freely give.
Payment is obligatory upon all. All the tithe of the land is the Lord’s: it is holy unto the Lord.

Malachi enforces the tithe with a charge the readings will not make: will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me, in tithes and offerings. The readings call the Ḥuqúq binding and forbid anyone to demand it. Can an obligation be real if no one may press it?
Collected only in joy and radiance. The people bring much more than enough, and Moses had to restrain them from bringing.
Nineteen mithqáls out of a hundred are God’s. The Qur’an’s share: a fifth thereof is for Allah, and for the messenger and for the kinsman and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer.
The Ḥuqúq pertains exclusively to God. The earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof.
To be allowed to offer it is a favour. Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow.
It is the cause of blessing. Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, and prove me now herewith, if I will not open you the windows of heaven.
A source of blessing for the giver; God is independent of it. Honour the Lord with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase: so shall thy barns be filled with plenty.
Malachi and Proverbs promise full barns. Jesus moved the reward: lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven. Which kind of blessing do the readings promise the one who pays?
Deduct the year’s expenses; the Ḥuqúq falls on the surplus. It is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.
Property that serves one’s needs is exempt. The third-year tithe was laid up within the gates for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.
Selling property to pay is not permitted. Jesus condemned the gift to God that left parents unprovided: ye say, it is Corban, and suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother.
The rich commanded to give, by an institution older than Moses. Melchizedek blessed Abram, who gave him tithes of all.
The Fifth, attributed to the kindred of the Messenger. Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s.
Payment accepted, solicitation forbidden. Paul to those who supported him: not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account.
The Ḥuqúq cannot be given to just anyone. It is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Give it to a trusted one and obtain a receipt. Paul on carrying the collection: providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
Those enabled to discharge it are remembered. The things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable.
Two-thirds to be spent on kindred and the poor. Righteous is he who giveth wealth, for love of Him, to kinsfolk and to orphans and the needy and the wayfarer.

Collect it, but require no one to pay. In Acts a gift misrepresented cost Ananias his life, though Peter granted that it was his own to keep: whiles it remained, was it not thine own? What is the offence in his story, and does the readings’ rule make it impossible?

A test to distinguish the friend from the stranger. Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone. How could exact payment become a way of failing the test?

shortfall: Most of the remaining readings are computations, receipts and messages to particular trustees; they need no companion and none was sought.

malachi-will-a-man-rob-god.text: Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings

leviticus-tithe-is-the-lords.text: And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the Lord's: it is holy unto the Lord

quran-a-fifth-thereof-is-for-allah.text: And know that whatever ye take as spoils of war, lo! a fifth thereof is for Allah, and for the messenger and for the kinsman (who hath need) and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer

philippians-not-because-i-desire-a-gift.text: Not because I desire a gift: but I desire fruit that may abound to your account

corinthians-providing-for-honest-things.text: Avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men
